content: High altitude illness (HAI) refers to a group of medical conditions, primarily affecting the brain and lungs, that can occur when individuals ascend to elevations above 2500 meters (approximately 8200 feet). These conditions include acute mountain sickness (AMS), high altitude cerebral edema (HACE), and high altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). This review focuses on the effectiveness and safety of five less commonly used pharmacological interventions for preventing HAI. The objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical efficacy and potential adverse effects of these five drug classes in individuals at risk of developing HAI. The drugs assessed include selective 5-hydroxytryptamine(1) receptor agonists, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonists, endothelin-1 antagonists, anticonvulsant drugs, and spironolactone. The review included randomized controlled trials where these medications were administered prior to ascent, excluding studies where the drugs were used during or after ascent. The search strategy involved multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of May 2017. Both thesaurus-based and free-text search terms were employed. Reference lists of included trials and relevant systematic reviews were also examined for additional studies. Eight studies, involving 334 participants, were included in this review. Twelve additional studies are ongoing, and another 12 studies are awaiting classification due to the unavailability of full-text versions. The included studies varied in methodological quality, with some demonstrating low risk of bias in randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding, while others exhibited high risk of selective reporting bias. The main findings are as follows: 1. Sumatriptan versus placebo: One study with 102 participants showed that sumatriptan reduced the risk of AMS compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] = 0.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21 to 0.84). However, the evidence quality was low. The study did not report on HAPE, HACE, or adverse events related to sumatriptan. 2. Magnesium citrate versus placebo: One study with 70 participants found no significant difference in the risk of AMS between magnesium citrate and placebo (RR = 1.09, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.13). However, magnesium citrate was associated with an increased risk of loose stools (RR = 3.25, 95% CI 1.17 to 8.99). The study did not report on HAPE or HACE. The evidence quality was low. 3. Spironolactone versus placebo: Two studies with 205 participants showed conflicting results for the risk of AMS, with one study reporting a reduced risk (RR = 0.40, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.31) and the other reporting an increased risk (RR = 1.44, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.01). Due to significant heterogeneity (I² = 72%), pooled analysis was not performed. No events of HAPE or HACE were reported, and adverse events were not evaluated. The evidence quality was very low. 4. Acetazolamide versus spironolactone: One study with 232 participants demonstrated that acetazolamide reduced the risk of AMS compared to spironolactone (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.70). No events of HAPE or HACE were reported, and adverse events were not evaluated. The evidence quality was low. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of these less commonly used pharmacological interventions for preventing HAI. The available data are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions due to the small number of studies, the low to very low quality of evidence, and the large number of studies that are either ongoing or awaiting classification. Further well-designed, large-scale studies are needed to establish the efficacy and safety of these pharmacological agents.
